warmup.q: A Netty echo handler calls ctx.write(msg) for every message, and the client reads ten times slower than it sends. What happens to the bytes the server can't send yet?
options: ctx.write blocks until the client catches up
Netty drops them and logs a warning
They queue in the channel's outbound buffer in your process, which keeps growing unless your code reacts
The kernel stores them all in the socket's send buffer
warmup.why: write never blocks the event loop. Netty queues the message in the channel's outbound buffer and writes it when the socket has room. The kernel's send buffer is small and fills first, so the rest piles up in your heap or direct memory. In this lesson's demo the queue peaked at 1.3 to 1.9 MB for 8 MiB of echo, and a test run of the same code saw the whole 16 MB payload waiting.

sections.html:
TCP delivers a stream of bytes, not messages (lesson 2). So the first job of any protocol pipeline is framing: finding where one message ends and the next begins. The payment link in this lesson's lab uses the most common framing for binary protocols, a length prefix:

[ length: int32 ][ type: int8 ][ body: UTF-8 bytes ]      length = 1 + body bytes

Here is a frame decoder written by hand. Netty's ByteToMessageDecoder is a handler that keeps every byte that has arrived so far in one buffer (Netty calls it the cumulation) and calls your decode each time more bytes arrive. Your job is to take out whole frames and leave the rest for later:

Java
class HandMadeFrameDecoder extends ByteToMessageDecoder {
    @Override
    protected void decode(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, ByteBuf in, List<Object> out) {
        if (in.readableBytes() < 4) return;              // 1. not even the length yet
        int length = in.getInt(in.readerIndex());        // 2. peek, don't consume
        if (length > 1020) throw new TooLongFrameException("frame too long: " + length);
        if (in.readableBytes() < 4 + length) return;     // 3. body incomplete: wait for more
        in.skipBytes(4);
        out.add(in.readRetainedSlice(length));           // 4. one whole frame, no copy
    }
}
Kotlin
class HandMadeFrameDecoder : ByteToMessageDecoder() {
    override fun decode(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext, input: ByteBuf, out: MutableList<Any>) {
        if (input.readableBytes() < 4) return            // 1. not even the length yet
        val length = input.getInt(input.readerIndex())   // 2. peek, don't consume
        if (length > 1020) throw TooLongFrameException("frame too long: $length")
        if (input.readableBytes() < 4 + length) return   // 3. body incomplete: wait for more
        input.skipBytes(4)
        out += input.readRetainedSlice(length)           // 4. one whole frame, no copy
    }
}

Each line follows a rule from the ByteToMessageDecoder Javadoc. Return without moving the reader index when a frame is incomplete. Use getInt(in.readerIndex()), not getInt(0), because the cumulation can still hold consumed bytes in front of the reader index. Hand the frame on as a slice, a view of the same memory, because readBytes(n) allocates a new buffer that someone must release. And never mark a ByteToMessageDecoder @Sharable: it keeps per-channel state.

You don't have to write it. new LengthFieldBasedFrameDecoder(1024, 0, 4, 0, 4) does the same job: frames of at most 1024 bytes, a length field at offset 0 that is 4 bytes long, no adjustment (the length counts only what follows it), and strip 4 bytes before passing the frame on. The figure shows each number on the wire. The next decoder sees exactly [type][body] and turns it into a PaymentMessage. On the way out, a MessageToByteEncoder<PaymentMessage> writes the three fields back.

The maximum is a security setting. A client that sends a length of two billion would make a decoder without one buffer two gigabytes while it waits. With it, the demo's hostile frame fails at once with Adjusted frame length exceeds 1024: 5004 - discarded (5,000 plus the 4-byte length field).

try.title: Feed a codec in awkward pieces
steps: Open CodecDemo.java (or CodecDemo.kt). It encodes two frames, 11 and 14 bytes long, and feeds them to a server pipeline cut at bytes 3, 9 and 14.
Predict which of the four slices produce a reply, and which reply.
Run it. Then change the cut at 9 to 11 and predict again.

code.html: package workbench.nio.l04; import io.netty.buffer.ByteBuf; import io.netty.buffer.ByteBufUtil; import io.netty.buffer.Unpooled; import io.netty.channel.ChannelHandlerContext; import io.netty.channel.SimpleChannelInboundHandler; import io.netty.channel.embedded.EmbeddedChannel; import io.netty.handler.codec.ByteToMessageDecoder; import io.netty.handler.codec.LengthFieldBasedFrameDecoder; import io.netty.handler.codec.MessageToByteEncoder; import io.netty.handler.codec.TooLongFrameException; import java.util.ArrayList; import java.util.List; import static java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets.UTF_8; /** A length-prefixed codec fed in awkward slices: [int length][byte type][UTF-8 text]. */ public class CodecDemo { record Frame(int type, String text) { } static final class FrameEncoder extends MessageToByteEncoder<Frame> { @Override protected void encode(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, Frame f, ByteBuf out) { byte[] text = f.text().getBytes(UTF_8); out.writeInt(1 + text.length).writeByte(f.type()).writeBytes(text); } } static final class FrameDecoder extends ByteToMessageDecoder { // runs after the length is stripped @Override protected void decode(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, ByteBuf in, List<Object> out) { int type = in.readByte(); out.add(new Frame(type, in.readCharSequence(in.readableBytes(), UTF_8).toString())); } } static final class Approver extends SimpleChannelInboundHandler<Frame> { @Override protected void channelRead0(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, Frame f) { ctx.writeAndFlush(new Frame(f.type() + 1, f.text().toUpperCase())); } } static EmbeddedChannel server() { return new EmbeddedChannel(new LengthFieldBasedFrameDecoder(1024, 0, 4, 0, 4), new FrameDecoder(), new FrameEncoder(), new Approver()); } public static void main(String[] args) { EmbeddedChannel encoder = new EmbeddedChannel(new FrameEncoder()); encoder.writeOutbound(new Frame(1, "auth-1"), new Frame(7, "capture-1")); ByteBuf wire = Unpooled.buffer(); ByteBuf part; while ((part = encoder.readOutbound()) != null) { wire.writeBytes(part); part.release(); } System.out.println("wire: " + wire.readableBytes() + " bytes, hex " + ByteBufUtil.hexDump(wire)); EmbeddedChannel ch = server(); int[] cuts = {3, 9, 14, wire.readableBytes()}; // inside the length, inside body 1, across the boundary, the rest int from = 0; for (int to : cuts) { ch.writeInbound(wire.retainedSlice(from, to - from)); List<String> replies = new ArrayList<>(); ByteBuf out; while ((out = ch.readOutbound()) != null) { replies.add("type=" + out.getByte(4) + " " + out.toString(5, out.readableBytes() - 5, UTF_8)); out.release(); } System.out.printf("bytes [%2d,%2d) -> replies %s%n", from, to, replies); from = to; } wire.release(); try { ch.writeInbound(Unpooled.buffer().writeInt(5_000).writeByte(1)); } catch (TooLongFrameException e) { System.out.println("length 5000 -> TooLongFrameException: " + e.getMessage()); } System.out.println("finish() = " + ch.finish()); } }

sections.h: A ByteBuf has two indexes and a reference count
sections.html:
Netty's ByteBuf fixes the two things that made ByteBuffer painful in lesson 2. It has separate readerIndex and writerIndex, so there is no read mode, no write mode and no flip(). And it is reference-counted, so Netty can pool its memory.

Pooling is the reason for the counting. Netty allocates direct memory, outside the Java heap, because the kernel can read it without a copy. Direct memory is costly to allocate, so Netty's allocator carves buffers out of big chunks and takes them back for reuse. The garbage collector can't do that hand-back: it frees an object at some unknown later time, when heap pressure says so, while a busy server needs the memory back the moment a message is done. So every ByteBuf carries a count. It starts at 1, retain() adds one, release() subtracts one, and at 0 the memory goes back to the pool. Touch the buffer after that and Netty throws:

buffer(16): AdaptiveByteBuf direct=true readerIndex=0 writerIndex=0 refCnt=1
after writeInt+writeLong: writerIndex=12 readableBytes=12
after readInt: readerIndex=4 readableBytes=8 (no flip)
retain(): refCnt=2
release() -> false, refCnt=1
release() -> true, refCnt=0 (memory goes back to the allocator)
readLong() after release -> IllegalReferenceCountException: refCnt: 0

AdaptiveByteBuf comes from the adaptive allocator, the default since Netty 4.2.

Who calls release()? Netty's wiki answers in one sentence: the party that accesses a reference-counted object last is responsible for destroying it. In a pipeline that works out as follows.

  • A handler that passes a message on with ctx.fireChannelRead(msg) hands over ownership and must not release it.
  • A handler that consumes a message and doesn't pass it on must release it. SimpleChannelInboundHandler does that for you after channelRead0 returns.
  • A message you write belongs to Netty, which releases it once it is on the wire.
  • A decoder that turns a buffer into something else releases the input. ByteToMessageDecoder and MessageToMessageDecoder do it for you.

Get it wrong one way and you release twice: IllegalReferenceCountException, loud and immediate. Get it wrong the other way and you leak pooled memory that never comes back, quietly, until the service runs out of direct memory.

import static java.nio.charset.StandardCharsets.US_ASCII; /** A ByteBuf's two indexes and its reference count, step by step. */ public class RefCountDemo { public static void main(String[] args) { System.out.println("default allocator: " + ByteBufAllocator.DEFAULT.getClass().getSimpleName()); ByteBuf b = ByteBufAllocator.DEFAULT.buffer(16); System.out.println("buffer(16): " + b.getClass().getSimpleName() + " direct=" + b.isDirect() + " readerIndex=" + b.readerIndex() + " writerIndex=" + b.writerIndex() + " refCnt=" + b.refCnt()); b.writeInt(42).writeLong(7); System.out.println("after writeInt+writeLong: writerIndex=" + b.writerIndex() + " readableBytes=" + b.readableBytes()); b.readInt(); System.out.println("after readInt: readerIndex=" + b.readerIndex() + " readableBytes=" + b.readableBytes() + " (no flip)"); b.retain(); System.out.println("retain(): refCnt=" + b.refCnt()); System.out.println("release() -> " + b.release() + ", refCnt=" + b.refCnt()); System.out.println("release() -> " + b.release() + ", refCnt=" + b.refCnt() + " (memory goes back to the allocator)"); try { b.readLong(); } catch (IllegalReferenceCountException e) { System.out.println("readLong() after release -> " + e.getClass().getSimpleName() + ": " + e.getMessage()); } ByteBuf header = Unpooled.copiedBuffer("HDR:", US_ASCII); ByteBuf body = Unpooled.copiedBuffer("payload", US_ASCII); CompositeByteBuf frame = Unpooled.compositeBuffer(); frame.addComponents(true, header, body); // no bytes copied; frame now owns both parts body.setByte(0, 'P'); System.out.println("composite: " + frame.toString(US_ASCII) + " (sees the change to body: shared memory)"); frame.release(); System.out.println("composite.release(): header.refCnt=" + header.refCnt() + " body.refCnt=" + body.refCnt()); try.expect: release() returns false while the count stays above 0 and true when it reaches 0. Reading after that throws IllegalReferenceCountException: refCnt: 0. The composite prints HDR:Payload: it shares memory with body, so the change made through body shows up without a copy. addComponents(true, ...) transferred ownership, so releasing the composite released both parts: header.refCnt=0 body.refCnt=0.

sections.h: PARANOID leak detection catches leaks in tests
sections.html:
A leaked ByteBuf doesn't throw. Netty finds leaks after the fact with ResourceLeakDetector. It attaches a weak reference to each buffer it tracks, and when the garbage collector collects a tracked buffer whose count never reached 0, the detector logs a report. Tracking costs time, so by default (the SIMPLE level) Netty tracks about 1 buffer in 128. ADVANCED samples the same way but also records where the buffer was touched. PARANOID tracks every buffer with full records, and the Netty wiki recommends it for tests. Turn it on with -Dio.netty.leakDetection.level=paranoid, or in a test with ResourceLeakDetector.setLevel(Level.PARANOID).

This is the start of the report from this section's demo, where a handler drops ten buffers without releasing them:

[main] ERROR io.netty.util.ResourceLeakDetector - LEAK: ByteBuf.release() was not called before it's garbage-collected. See https://netty.io/wiki/reference-counted-objects.html for more information.
Recent access records:
#1:
	Hint: 'LeakDemo$1#0' will handle the message from this point.
	...
Created at:
	io.netty.buffer.AdaptiveByteBufAllocator.newDirectBuffer(AdaptiveByteBufAllocator.java:67)
	...
10 buffers leaked; the listener saw 1 report(s): [ByteBuf]

Read it from the bottom. Created at is where the buffer was allocated, and the access records show who touched it last: the hint names the handler that received it and never let go. Ten buffers leaked, yet there is one report, because the detector reports each distinct access path once.

To fail a build on a leak you need two more pieces. ByteBufUtil.setLeakListener(...) gives you a callback per report, so a test can collect them. And detection needs a garbage collection followed by another allocation, because the detector checks its queue of collected buffers when it tracks the next one. The lab's last test does exactly that:

Java
for (int i = 0; i < 40 && leaks.isEmpty(); i++) {
    System.gc();                                    // collect the leaked ByteBuf objects
    Thread.sleep(20);
    ByteBufAllocator.DEFAULT.buffer(8).release();   // the next allocation reports them
}
assertThat(leaks).isEmpty();
Kotlin
var i = 0
while (i++ < 40 && leaks.isEmpty()) {
    System.gc()                                     // collect the leaked ByteBuf objects
    Thread.sleep(20)
    ByteBufAllocator.DEFAULT.buffer(8).release()    // the next allocation reports them
}
assertThat(leaks).isEmpty()

GC timing makes this check probabilistic, so pair it with a deterministic one: keep a reference to the buffer you pushed in, and assert refCnt() == 0 after the pipeline ran. The lab does both.

PARANOID leak detection reports it. */ public class LeakDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { ResourceLeakDetector.setLevel(ResourceLeakDetector.Level.PARANOID); // track every buffer List<String> leaks = new CopyOnWriteArrayList<>(); ByteBufUtil.setLeakListener((type, records) -> leaks.add(type)); EmbeddedChannel ch = new EmbeddedChannel(new ChannelInboundHandlerAdapter() { @Override public void channelRead(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, Object msg) { // BUG: neither released nor passed on with ctx.fireChannelRead(msg) } }); for (int i = 0; i < 10; i++) { ByteBuf m = ByteBufAllocator.DEFAULT.buffer(32); m.writeInt(i); ch.writeInbound(m); } ch.finishAndReleaseAll(); // a leak is noticed when the buffer object is garbage-collected while refCnt > 0, // and reported on a later allocation for (int i = 0; i < 40 && leaks.isEmpty(); i++) { System.gc(); Thread.sleep(20); ByteBufAllocator.DEFAULT.buffer(8).release(); } Thread.sleep(100); System.out.println("10 buffers leaked; the listener saw " + leaks.size() + " report(s): " + leaks); } }

sections.h: Flow control: stop reading when you can't write
sections.html:
ctx.write(msg) never blocks, and a slow client never makes it fail. Netty puts the message in the channel's outbound buffer, a queue in your own process's memory, and moves it to the socket when the kernel's send buffer has room. That is handy, and it is also how a Netty service runs out of memory: if the peer reads more slowly than you write, the queue grows without limit.

Netty tells you when the queue gets long. Each channel has two water marks, 32 KiB low and 64 KiB high by default (WriteBufferWaterMark). When the bytes waiting in the outbound buffer pass the high mark, channel.isWritable() turns false and Netty fires channelWritabilityChanged. When they drain below the low mark, isWritable() turns true and the event fires again. Two marks instead of one stop it from flipping on every write.

Netty doesn't stop your writes when isWritable() is false. You have to act. For an echo server or a proxy, the action is lesson 2's: stop reading from whoever produces the data. setAutoRead(false) tells the event loop to stop reading that channel, which for the NIO transport means taking OP_READ out of its interest set:

Java
@Override
public void channelReadComplete(ChannelHandlerContext ctx) {
    ctx.flush();
    if (!ctx.channel().isWritable()) ctx.channel().config().setAutoRead(false);   // stop reading
}

@Override
public void channelWritabilityChanged(ChannelHandlerContext ctx) {
    if (ctx.channel().isWritable()) ctx.channel().config().setAutoRead(true);      // drained: read again
    ctx.fireChannelWritabilityChanged();
}
Kotlin
override fun channelReadComplete(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext) {
    ctx.flush()
    if (!ctx.channel().isWritable) ctx.channel().config().isAutoRead = false      // stop reading
}

override fun channelWritabilityChanged(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext) {
    if (ctx.channel().isWritable) ctx.channel().config().isAutoRead = true         // drained: read again
    ctx.fireChannelWritabilityChanged()
}

This section's demo echoes 8 MiB to a client that writes fast and reads slowly. Without those two methods, the outbound buffer peaked at 1,905,344 bytes in one run and 1,332,000 in another, and a test run of the same code for this track saw 16,202,075: the whole payload. With them, the peak was about 129,000 bytes every time. In a proxy you wire it across two channels: the backend's writability switches the frontend's auto-read.

Two more traps showed up while measuring this. Calling close() right after the last flush() lost 57,344 bytes that were still in the outbound buffer. Close from the write's future instead: ctx.writeAndFlush(last).addListener(ChannelFutureListener.CLOSE). And channelWritabilityChanged can fire inside your own flush() call, so a handler that writes from that event must cope with being called while it is already writing.

try.title: Measure the queue
steps: Lower the water marks: add .childOption(ChannelOption.WRITE_BUFFER_WATER_MARK, new WriteBufferWaterMark(8 * 1024, 16 * 1024)) to the server bootstrap. Predict the new peak with backpressure: about a quarter of the old one?
Run it and explain the number. Where in the handler is writability checked?

code.title: BackpressureDemo.java
code.html: package workbench.nio.l04; import io.netty.bootstrap.ServerBootstrap; import io.netty.channel.Channel; import io.netty.channel.ChannelHandlerContext; import io.netty.channel.ChannelInboundHandlerAdapter; import io.netty.channel.ChannelInitializer; import io.netty.channel.ChannelOption; import io.netty.channel.EventLoopGroup; import io.netty.channel.MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup; import io.netty.channel.nio.NioIoHandler; import io.netty.channel.socket.SocketChannel; import io.netty.channel.socket.nio.NioServerSocketChannel; import java.io.IOException; import java.io.InputStream; import java.io.OutputStream; import java.net.InetAddress; import java.net.Socket; import java.util.concurrent.TimeUnit; import java.util.concurrent.atomic.AtomicLong; /** * An echo server and a client that writes 8 MiB fast but reads slowly. How much piles up in the * server's outbound buffer, with and without backpressure? */ public class BackpressureDemo { public static void main(String[] args) throws Exception { for (boolean backpressure : new boolean[] {false, true}) { System.out.printf("backpressure=%-5s -> peak bytes waiting in the outbound buffer: %,d%n", backpressure, peakPending(backpressure, 8)); } } static long peakPending(boolean backpressure, int megabytes) throws Exception { EventLoopGroup group = new MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(1, NioIoHandler.newFactory()); AtomicLong peak = new AtomicLong(); try { Channel server = new ServerBootstrap().group(group).channel(NioServerSocketChannel.class) .childOption(ChannelOption.SO_SNDBUF, 32 * 1024) .childOption(ChannelOption.SO_RCVBUF, 32 * 1024) .childHandler(new ChannelInitializer<SocketChannel>() { @Override protected void initChannel(SocketChannel ch) { ch.pipeline().addLast(new ChannelInboundHandlerAdapter() { @Override public void channelRead(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, Object msg) { ctx.write(msg); // queue the echo in the outbound buffer long pending = ctx.channel().unsafe().outboundBuffer().totalPendingWriteBytes(); peak.accumulateAndGet(pending, Math::max); } @Override public void channelReadComplete(ChannelHandlerContext ctx) { ctx.flush(); if (backpressure && !ctx.channel().isWritable()) { ctx.channel().config().setAutoRead(false); // stop reading from a peer we can't write to } } @Override public void channelWritabilityChanged(ChannelHandlerContext ctx) { if (backpressure && ctx.channel().isWritable()) { ctx.channel().config().setAutoRead(true); // drained below the low water mark } ctx.fireChannelWritabilityChanged(); } }); } }) .bind(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), 0).sync().channel(); int total = megabytes << 20; try (Socket s = new Socket()) { s.setReceiveBufferSize(32 * 1024); s.setSendBufferSize(32 * 1024); s.connect(server.localAddress()); Thread writer = new Thread(() -> { // the fast writer try { OutputStream out = s.getOutputStream(); byte[] chunk = new byte[64 * 1024]; for (int i = 0; i < total / chunk.length; i++) out.write(chunk); s.shutdownOutput(); } catch (IOException ignored) { } }); writer.start(); InputStream in = s.getInputStream(); // the slow reader: 20 ms pause per 128 KiB byte[] buf = new byte[16 * 1024]; long got = 0; int n; while (got < total && (n = in.read(buf)) >= 0) { got += n; if ((got & ((128 << 10) - 1)) < n) Thread.sleep(20); } writer.join(); } server.close().sync(); } finally { group.shutdownGracefully(0, 1, TimeUnit.SECONDS).sync(); } return peak.get(); } }

How much piles up in the * server's outbound buffer, with and without backpressure? */ fun main() { for (backpressure in listOf(false, true)) { println("backpressure=%-5s -> peak bytes waiting in the outbound buffer: %,d".format(backpressure, peakPending(backpressure, 8))) } } private fun peakPending(backpressure: Boolean, megabytes: Int): Long { val group = MultiThreadIoEventLoopGroup(1, NioIoHandler.newFactory()) val peak = AtomicLong() try { val server = ServerBootstrap().group(group).channel(NioServerSocketChannel::class.java) .childOption(ChannelOption.SO_SNDBUF, 32 * 1024) .childOption(ChannelOption.SO_RCVBUF, 32 * 1024) .childHandler(object : ChannelInitializer<SocketChannel>() { override fun initChannel(ch: SocketChannel) { ch.pipeline().addLast(object : ChannelInboundHandlerAdapter() { override fun channelRead(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext, msg: Any) { ctx.write(msg) // queue the echo in the outbound buffer val pending = ctx.channel().unsafe().outboundBuffer().totalPendingWriteBytes() peak.accumulateAndGet(pending) { a, b -> maxOf(a, b) } } override fun channelReadComplete(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext) { ctx.flush() if (backpressure && !ctx.channel().isWritable) { ctx.channel().config().isAutoRead = false // stop reading from a peer we can't write to } } override fun channelWritabilityChanged(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext) { if (backpressure && ctx.channel().isWritable) { ctx.channel().config().isAutoRead = true // drained below the low water mark } ctx.fireChannelWritabilityChanged() } }) } }) .bind(InetAddress.getLoopbackAddress(), 0).sync().channel() val total = megabytes shl 20 Socket().use { s -> s.receiveBufferSize = 32 * 1024 s.sendBufferSize = 32 * 1024 s.connect(server.localAddress()) val writer = thread { // the fast writer try { val out = s.getOutputStream() val chunk = ByteArray(64 * 1024) repeat(total / chunk.size) { out.write(chunk) } s.shutdownOutput() } catch (_: IOException) { } } val input = s.getInputStream() // the slow reader: 20 ms pause per 128 KiB val buf = ByteArray(16 * 1024) var got = 0L while (got < total) { val n = input.read(buf) if (n < 0) break got += n if ((got and ((128L shl 10) - 1)) < n) Thread.sleep(20) } writer.join() } server.close().sync() } finally { group.shutdownGracefully(0, 1, TimeUnit.SECONDS).sync() } return peak.get() }

try.expect: Without backpressure the peak is in the megabytes and changes every run; with it, about 129,000 bytes. With a 16 KiB high mark the peak only fell to 113,536 bytes in my runs, nowhere near a quarter. The handler checks isWritable() in channelReadComplete, which runs once after a whole batch of reads, so most of the peak is that one batch arriving before auto-read is switched off. Checking in channelRead as well would stop the batch early.

analogy: The outbound buffer is a bathtub with the drain open and two marks painted on the side. Your handler is the tap. The drain is the socket, and it empties only as fast as the client reads. When the water passes the high mark you turn the tap off (auto-read off), and when it falls below the low mark you turn it back on. Leave the tap running and the bathroom floods. The analogy breaks at the tap: turning it off doesn't waste water. The client's data waits upstream, in the kernel's buffers and the client's own send buffer, and TCP slows the client down for you.
world: Card networks and acquirer hosts often speak ISO 8583 over long-lived TCP connections, framed with a short binary length header in front of each message. That is LengthFieldBasedFrameDecoder territory, as the worked example shows: a 2-byte length is (maxLength, 0, 2, 0, 2), and a length that counts its own two bytes needs a lengthAdjustment of -2. If such a gateway runs on Netty or Vert.x, a missing release() shows up weeks later as direct memory that only grows, until buffer allocations fail with an out-of-direct-memory error. Run the gateway's pipeline tests at PARANOID, and give every channel that forwards to a slower system writability-based backpressure.
mistake: The common leak is a handler that does a little work on a buffer and then forgets whose it is. An audit or logging handler calls msg.copy() or msg.toString(UTF_8), passes a copy on, and never releases the original: that is this lesson's lab. The mirror image is a handler that extends SimpleChannelInboundHandler<ByteBuf> and also calls ctx.fireChannelRead(msg): the base class releases the buffer when channelRead0 returns, so the next handler reads freed memory and gets IllegalReferenceCountException. Pass the same buffer on with ChannelInboundHandlerAdapter and fireChannelRead(msg), or call ReferenceCountUtil.retain(msg) before passing it on from a SimpleChannelInboundHandler.

compare.title: The payment frame encoder and decoder

java.title: PaymentFrameCodec.java
java.html: class PaymentFrameEncoder extends MessageToByteEncoder<PaymentMessage> { @Override protected void encode(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, PaymentMessage msg, ByteBuf out) { byte[] body = msg.body().getBytes(UTF_8); out.writeInt(1 + body.length).writeByte(msg.type()).writeBytes(body); } } class PaymentFrameDecoder extends ByteToMessageDecoder { @Override protected void decode(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, ByteBuf in, List<Object> out) { int type = in.readByte(); out.add(new PaymentMessage(type, in.readCharSequence(in.readableBytes(), UTF_8).toString())); } }

kotlin.title: PaymentFrameCodec.kt
kotlin.html: class PaymentFrameEncoder : MessageToByteEncoder<PaymentMessage>() { override fun encode(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext, msg: PaymentMessage, out: ByteBuf) { val body = msg.body.toByteArray(UTF_8) out.writeInt(1 + body.size).writeByte(msg.type).writeBytes(body) } } class PaymentFrameDecoder : ByteToMessageDecoder() { override fun decode(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext, input: ByteBuf, out: MutableList<Any>) { val type = input.readByte().toInt() out += PaymentMessage(type, input.readCharSequence(input.readableBytes(), UTF_8).toString()) } }

compare.note: The runtime behavior is identical; the differences are names and types. Java's decoder parameter is called in, which is a keyword in Kotlin, so the Kotlin override renames it (input), which overriding allows. readByte() returns a Byte in Kotlin, and Kotlin never widens it to Int implicitly, so you write .toInt() where Java widens silently. The out list is a Java List<Object>, which Kotlin sees as MutableList<Any>. Getters such as isWritable() and isAutoRead() become properties (isWritable, isAutoRead = false) in Kotlin. Reference counting is the same in both: Kotlin's use {} does not help, because ByteBuf is not AutoCloseable.

worked.title: Frame an ISO 8583 style link with a 2-byte length

steps.say: An acquirer link sends each message behind a 2-byte big-endian length that counts only the bytes after it. Frames are at most 4,096 bytes. Ask four questions: where is the length, how long is it, what does it count, and do you keep it?
steps.code:
wire:   00 08 | 30 31 30 30 61 75 74 68      (length 8, then "0100auth")
offset: 0               the length starts the frame
length: 2 bytes
counts: what follows    lengthAdjustment 0
keep:   no              initialBytesToStrip 2

steps.say: That gives the decoder's arguments. LengthFieldPrepender is the matching encoder: it writes the length in front of every outbound buffer, so the business handler never deals with the header.
steps.code: ch.pipeline().addLast( new LengthFieldBasedFrameDecoder(4096, 0, 2, 0, 2), // 1. frame inbound, strip the header new LengthFieldPrepender(2), // 2. add the header outbound new Iso8583Codec(), // 3. bytes <-> messages new AuthorizationHandler());

alt.html: ch.pipeline().addLast( LengthFieldBasedFrameDecoder(4096, 0, 2, 0, 2), // 1. frame inbound, strip the header LengthFieldPrepender(2), // 2. add the header outbound Iso8583Codec(), // 3. bytes <-> messages AuthorizationHandler())

steps.say: A second acquirer counts the 2 header bytes in the length: the same message arrives as 00 0a .... The decoder computes the frame size as header end plus the length value plus lengthAdjustment, so subtract the 2 bytes the value already includes. The prepender has a flag for the same convention.
steps.code: new LengthFieldBasedFrameDecoder(4096, 0, 2, -2, 2), // 10 - 2 = 8 body bytes new LengthFieldPrepender(2, true) // write 2 + body length

alt.html: LengthFieldBasedFrameDecoder(4096, 0, 2, -2, 2) // 10 - 2 = 8 body bytes LengthFieldPrepender(2, true) // write 2 + body length

steps.say: Prove it with an EmbeddedChannel before you connect to anything: write one message out, feed the bytes back in split after the first byte, and expect the original. A wrong adjustment shows up here as a frame that never completes or one that swallows the next message's header.
steps.code: EmbeddedChannel ch = new EmbeddedChannel( new LengthFieldBasedFrameDecoder(4096, 0, 2, -2, 2), new LengthFieldPrepender(2, true)); ch.writeOutbound(Unpooled.copiedBuffer("0100auth", UTF_8)); ByteBuf wire = ch.readOutbound(); // 00 0a 30 31 30 30 61 75 74 68 ch.writeInbound(wire.retainedSlice(0, 1)); // half a header: nothing yet ch.writeInbound(wire.retainedSlice(1, wire.readableBytes() - 1)); wire.release(); ByteBuf frame = ch.readInbound(); // "0100auth" frame.release();

alt.html: val ch = EmbeddedChannel( LengthFieldBasedFrameDecoder(4096, 0, 2, -2, 2), LengthFieldPrepender(2, true)) ch.writeOutbound(Unpooled.copiedBuffer("0100auth", UTF_8)) val wire = ch.readOutbound<ByteBuf>() // 00 0a 30 31 30 30 61 75 74 68 ch.writeInbound(wire.retainedSlice(0, 1)) // half a header: nothing yet ch.writeInbound(wire.retainedSlice(1, wire.readableBytes() - 1)) wire.release() val frame = ch.readInbound<ByteBuf>() // "0100auth" frame.release()

lab.title: Write a payment frame codec and find a leak
steps: Run the tests. All five fail. Read PaymentMessage.java for the wire format.
Write PaymentFrameEncoder.encode: the length (1 + body bytes) as an int, the type as a byte, then the UTF-8 body.
Write PaymentFrameDecoder.decode: read the type byte, then the rest as UTF-8 with readCharSequence, and add one PaymentMessage to out. Then PaymentCodec.handlers. The first three tests should pass.
Fix AuditTap so the buffer that arrived is the one that goes on. The last two tests should pass.
Now make a leak on purpose: in the decoder, read the body with in.readBytes(in.readableBytes()).toString(UTF_8). Run the tests and see which one fails, and why only that one. Put it back.
hints: The first test prints the bytes as hex: 00000007 is the length, 01 the type, and 617574682d31 is auth-1 in ASCII.
in.readCharSequence(n, UTF_8) decodes in place and moves the reader index. in.readBytes(n) allocates a new ByteBuf, and nobody releases it.
The AuditTap test fails with a reference count of 1: the buffer that arrived was never released, because a copy went on in its place.
The test class sets PARANOID in @BeforeAll and puts the default back in @AfterAll. The leak test runs last, so it also catches leaks from the earlier tests.
lab.done: All five tests in PaymentCodecTest pass, and you have seen the PARANOID test catch the readBytes leak.

drill.title: Write the backpressure pair from memory
drill.prompt: Close this page. In a ChannelInboundHandlerAdapter for an echo server, write the two methods that stop reading while the channel isn't writable and start again when it drains. Which default water marks decide when each one fires?

answer.html: @Override public void channelRead(ChannelHandlerContext ctx, Object msg) { ctx.write(msg); // ownership moves to the write } @Override public void channelReadComplete(ChannelHandlerContext ctx) { ctx.flush(); if (!ctx.channel().isWritable()) ctx.channel().config().setAutoRead(false); } @Override public void channelWritabilityChanged(ChannelHandlerContext ctx) { if (ctx.channel().isWritable()) ctx.channel().config().setAutoRead(true); ctx.fireChannelWritabilityChanged(); } // isWritable() turns false above the 64 KiB high water mark, true again below the 32 KiB low mark.

alt.html: override fun channelRead(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext, msg: Any) { ctx.write(msg) // ownership moves to the write } override fun channelReadComplete(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext) { ctx.flush() if (!ctx.channel().isWritable) ctx.channel().config().isAutoRead = false } override fun channelWritabilityChanged(ctx: ChannelHandlerContext) { if (ctx.channel().isWritable) ctx.channel().config().isAutoRead = true ctx.fireChannelWritabilityChanged() } // isWritable turns false above the 64 KiB high water mark, true again below the 32 KiB low mark.

recap: Frame before you decode. LengthFieldBasedFrameDecoder(max, offset, length, adjustment, strip) turns a byte stream into whole frames and rejects frames above max.
A ByteToMessageDecoder returns without consuming when a frame is incomplete, uses readerIndex()-relative access, is never @Sharable, and hands frames on as slices, not readBytes copies.
A ByteBuf has separate reader and writer indexes and a reference count. The last party to touch it releases it; passing it on transfers ownership.
Leaks are found when a tracked buffer is garbage-collected with a count above 0. Run tests at PARANOID with a leak listener and a GC loop, and pair it with a refCnt() == 0 assertion.
write queues in the outbound buffer without limit. Watch isWritable() (64 KiB high, 32 KiB low by default) and turn auto-read off while the peer can't keep up.
Close after the last write completes (ChannelFutureListener.CLOSE), not right after flush().

explain.prompt: Explain why Netty's ByteBuf needs release() even though the JVM has a garbage collector, and how you would make sure a pipeline doesn't leak.
explain.answer: Netty allocates direct memory outside the heap so the kernel can use it without a copy, and because that memory is expensive to allocate, Netty pools it: buffers are slices of big chunks that go back to the pool for reuse. The garbage collector would free a buffer object at some unknown later time, which is far too late and can't return a pooled slice anyway. So each buffer has a reference count, and the party that touches it last releases it. In a pipeline, handlers that pass a message on hand over ownership, handlers that consume it release it (SimpleChannelInboundHandler does it for you), and Netty releases what you write. To make sure nothing leaks, I'd run the pipeline tests with leak detection at PARANOID, install a leak listener, force garbage collection and an allocation at the end, and assert there were no reports. I'd also assert refCnt() == 0 on the buffers I pushed in, which catches the common case deterministically.

deeper.html:
A few ByteToMessageDecoder details explain behavior you will see in profiles.

The default cumulator, MERGE_CUMULATOR, copies newly read bytes into one growing buffer. COMPOSITE_CUMULATOR adds them as components instead and avoids the copy, but the Javadoc warns it may be slower, because reading across component boundaries costs more. The decoder also compacts the cumulation after 16 reads (discardAfterReads), so a long-lived connection doesn't keep consumed bytes forever. setSingleDecode(true) makes it produce at most one message per read, which matters when you control reading yourself.

That leads to FlowControlHandler. With auto-read off you call ctx.read() to ask for one more read, but a decoder can still emit many messages from that one read, because one read can contain many frames. Its Javadoc says FlowControlHandler "ensures that only one message per read() is sent downstream". Put it after your decoders when you need strict one-request-at-a-time processing per connection.

On allocators: io.netty.allocator.type picks adaptive (the 4.2 default), pooled or unpooled. The adaptive allocator keeps several "magazines" of memory, picks one by thread id, and adds magazines when it sees contention. The older pooled allocator keeps per-thread caches, and its useCacheForAllThreads setting defaults to false, which suggests that buffers allocated on your own executor threads miss those caches. That last point is an inference from the property name and default, not something this track measured.

Finally, production: leave the level at SIMPLE. It samples 1 buffer in 128, so a leak on a busy path still reaches the logs, while the other 127 buffers pay nothing for tracking.
